Et ideo simpliciter dicendum est, quod peccatum traducitur per originem a primo parente in posteros. Ad cuius evidentiam considerandum est, quod aliquis homo singularis dupliciter potest considerari: uno modo secundum quod est quaedam persona singularis; alio modo secundum quod est pars alicuius collegii, et utroque modo ad eum potest aliquis actus pertinere. Pertinet enim ad eum in quantum est singularis persona, ille actus quem proprio arbitrio et per se ipsum facit; sed in quantum est pars collegii, potest ad eum pertinere actus aliquis quem per se ipsum non facit nec proprio arbitrio, sed qui fit a toto collegio vel a pluribus de collegio vel a principe collegii; sicut illud quod princeps civitatis facit, dicitur civitas facere, ut philosophus dicit. Huiusmodi enim collegium hominum reputatur quasi unus homo, ita quod diversi homines in diversis officiis constituti sunt quasi diversa membra unius corporis naturalis, ut apostolus inducit de membris Ecclesiae, I Cor. XII, 12. Sic ergo tota multitudo hominum a primo parente humanam naturam accipientium, quasi unum collegium, vel potius sicut unum corpus unius hominis consideranda est; in qua quidem multitudo unusquisque homo, etiam ipse Adam, potest considerari vel quasi singularis persona, vel quasi aliquod membrum huius multitudinis, quae per naturalem originem derivatur ab uno. Est autem considerandum quod primo homini in sua institutione datum fuerat divinitus quoddam supernaturale donum, scilicet originalis iustitia, per quam ratio subdebatur Deo, et inferiores vires rationi, et corpus animae. Hoc autem donum non fuerat datum primo homini ut singulari personae tantum, sed ut cuidam principio totius humanae naturae, ut scilicet ab eo per originem derivaretur in posteros. Hoc autem donum acceptum primus homo per liberum arbitrium peccans amisit eo tenore quo sibi datum fuerat, scilicet pro se et pro tota sua posteritate. Defectus ergo huius doni totam eius posteritatem consequitur; et sic iste defectus eo modo traducitur in posteros quo modo traducitur humana natura; quae quidem traducitur non quidem secundum se totam, sed secundum aliquam sui partem, scilicet secundum carnem, cui Deus animam infundit; et sic sicut anima divinitus infusa pertinet ad naturam humanam ab Adam derivatam, propter carnem cui coniungitur; ita et defectus praedictus pertinet ad animam propter carnem, quae ab Adam propagatur non solum secundum corpulentam substantiam, sed etiam secundum seminalem rationem, id est non solum materialiter, sed sicut ab activo principio: sic enim filius accipit a patre naturam humanam. Si ergo consideretur iste defectus hoc modo per originem in istum hominem derivatus, secundum illud quod iste homo est quaedam persona singularis, sic huiusmodi defectus, non potest habere rationem culpae, ad cuius rationem requiritur quod sit voluntaria. Sed si consideretur iste homo generatus sicut quoddam membrum totius humanae naturae a primo parente propagatae, ac si omnes homines essent unus homo, sic habet rationem culpae propter voluntarium eius principium, quod est actuale peccatum primi parentis; sicut si dicamus, quod motus manus ad homicidium perpetrandum, secundum quod manus per se consideratur, non habet rationem culpae, quia manus de necessitate movetur ab alio. Si autem consideretur ut est pars totius hominis, qui voluntate agit, sic habet rationem culpae, quia sic est voluntarius. Sicut ergo homicidium non dicitur culpa manus, sed culpa totius hominis; ita huiusmodi defectus non dicitur esse peccatum personale, sed peccatum totius naturae; nec ad personam pertinet, nisi in quantum natura inficit personam. Et sicut ad unum peccatum faciendum diversae partes hominis adhibentur, scilicet voluntas, ratio, manus et huiusmodi, et tamen est unum solum peccatum propter unitatem principii, scilicet voluntatis, a quo peccati ratio ad omnes actus partium derivatur; ita et ratione principii in tota natura humana consideratur quasi unum peccatum originale; propter quod apostolus dicit, Rom. V, 12: in quo omnes peccaverunt; quod secundum Augustinum, potest intelligi in quo scilicet primo homine, vel in quo peccato primi hominis, ut peccatum primi hominis sit quasi commune peccatum omnium. [61934] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 1 Ad primum ergo dicendum, quod peccatum quod per originem contrahitur, dicitur voluntarium ratione sui principii, scilicet voluntatis primi parentis, ut dictum est. [61935] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 2 Ad secundum dicendum, quod istud peccatum consequitur totam naturam humanam; unde subiectum huius peccati est anima, secundum quod est pars humanae naturae: et ideo sicut humana natura traducitur, licet anima non traducatur; ita etiam peccatum originale traducitur, licet anima non traducatur. [61936] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 3 Ad tertium dicendum, quod caro non est sufficiens causa peccati actualis, sed peccati originalis est sufficiens causa; sicut et traductio carnis est sufficiens causa, materialiter tamen, humanae naturae. [61937] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 4 Ad quartum dicendum, quod ei quod est per originem contractum, non debetur poena et increpatio si referatur ad personam, quia sic non habet rationem voluntarii, sed si referatur ad naturam, sic habet rationem voluntarii, ut dictum est et hoc modo debetur ei increpatio et poena. [61938] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 5 Ad quintum dicendum, quod defectus per originem contractus habet quidem rationem existentis ab alio, si referatur ad personam, non autem si referatur ad naturam; sic enim est quasi a principio intrinseco. [61939] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 6 Ad sextum dicendum, quod caro nostra in sui natura bona est, sed secundum quod est privata originali iustitia propter peccatum primi parentis, sic causat originale peccatum. [61940] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 7 Ad septimum dicendum, quod sicut dictum est, peccatum originale per se loquendo est peccatum naturae, non personae, nisi ratione naturae infectae. Actus autem generationis proprie deservit naturae, quia ordinatur ad conservationem speciei; sed carnem iam esse animae unitam pertinet ad constitutionem personae; et ideo caro magis causat originale peccatum prout consideratur in via generationis quam prout est iam unita. [61941] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 8 Ad octavum dicendum, quod in illis qui nascuntur ex fornicatione, est quidem origo dupliciter vitiata, vitio scilicet naturae, quod traducitur ex Adam, et vitio personae, id est patris generantis, ex quo vitio nulla infectio in prole relinquitur. Quilibet enim generans traducit peccatum originale in quantum generat ut Adam, non in quantum generat ut Petrus vel Martinus; id est per id quod habet ab Adam, non per id quod est proprium sibi. [61942] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 9 Ad nonum dicendum, quod corruptio quae est in carne, est quidem actus naturalis, sed intentione et virtute moralis. Ex peccato enim primi parentis destituta est caro eius illa virtute ut ex ea possit decidi semen per quod originalis iustitia in alios propagetur; et sic in semine defectus huius virtutis est defectus moralis corruptionis, et quaedam intentio eius; sicut dicimus intentionem coloris esse in aere, et intentionem animae esse in semine. Et ex hoc etiam est ibi virtus ad similem imperfectionem, sicut est ibi virtus ad productionem humanae naturae in prole generata. [61943] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 10 Ad decimum dicendum, quod nihil prohibet a causa spirituali causari effectum corporalem. Nam et Boetius dicit in libro de Trinitate quod formae quae sunt in materia, venerunt a formis quae sunt sine materia: et in nobis ipsis a voluntate movetur inferior appetitus, ad cuius motum sequitur transmutatio corporalis. [61944] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 11 Ad undecimum dicendum, quod originalis iustitia fuit superaddita primo homini ex liberalitate divina; sed quod huic animae non detur a Deo, non est ex parte eius, sed ex parte humanae naturae, in qua invenitur contrarium prohibens. [61945] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 12 Ad duodecimum dicendum, quod in semine est corruptio originalis peccati non actu sed virtute, eo modo quo est ibi virtute humana natura: quae quidem virtus activa in semine est in spiritu spumoso, ut Aristoteles dicit in Lib. de Gener. animalium, non autem in materia quae amittit unam formam et recipit aliam. [61946] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 13 Ad decimumtertium dicendum, quod sicut Dionysius dicit IV cap. de Div. Nom., bonum contingit ex tota integra causa, sed malum provenit etiam ex singularibus defectibus; et ideo defectus qui est ex parte corporis sufficit ad integritatem humanae naturae tollendam. [61947] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 14 Ad decimumquartum dicendum, quod carentia divinae visionis dupliciter competit alicui. Uno modo sic quod non habeat in se unde possit ad divinam visionem pervenire, et sic carentia divinae visionis competeret ei qui in solis naturalibus esset etiam absque peccato; sic enim carentia divinae visionis non est poena, sed defectus consequens omnem naturam creatam: quia nulla creatura ex suis naturalibus potest pervenire ad visionem divinam. Alio modo potest alicui competere carentia divinae visionis hoc modo ut habeat in se aliquid ex quo debeatur ei quod careat visione divina; et sic carentia visionis divinae est poena et originalis et actualis peccati. [61948] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 15 Ad decimumquintum dicendum, quod duplex est causa. Una principalis quae agit per propriam formam, et haec est nobilior quam effectus in quantum est causa. Alia est causa instrumentalis quae non agit per formam propriam, sed in quantum est mota ab alio, et hanc non oportet nobiliorem esse effectu, sicut serra non est nobilior quam domus. Hoc autem modo semen carnale est causa naturae humanae in prole, et etiam culpae originalis in anima eius. [61949] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 16 Ad decimumsextum dicendum, quod aliquod agens est in actu multipliciter. Uno modo secundum propriam formam, quae vel continet formam effectus secundum similitudinem speciei, sicut ignis generat ignem; vel secundum virtutem tantum, sicut sol generat ignem. Alio modo, secundum motum ab alio; et hoc modo instrumentum agit ut ens actu: et sic etiam semen est actu, in quantum est in eo motus et intentio animae generantis, secundum philosophum in Lib. de Gener. animalium; et ex hoc habet virtutem causandi et humanam naturam et originale peccatum. [61950] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 17 Ad decimumseptimum dicendum, quod aliquis vir iustus accedendo ad uxorem meretur secundum id quod est proprium sibi; et sic non transmittit peccatum originale, sed secundum id quod habet ab Adam, ut supra dictum est. [61951] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 18 Ad decimumoctavum dicendum, quod Adam in quantum fuit principium humanae naturae, habuit rationem causae universalis, et ita per eius actum corrupta est tota humana natura, quae ab eo propagatur. [61952] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 ad 19 Ad decimumnonum dicendum, quod peccatum primi hominis est quodammodo peccatum commune totius humanae naturae, ut dictum est; et ideo cum aliquis punitur pro peccato primi parentis, non punitur pro peccato alterius, sed pro peccato suo.

[61911] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 tit. 2 And it seems not.

[61912] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 1 For it is called Ecclesi. 15, 18: before man life and death, good and evil: whatsoever he will, it shall be given him. From this it may be understood that sin, which is the spiritual death of the soul, consists in the will. But nothing that man contracts from his origin consists in his will. Therefore man contracts no sin from his origin.

[61913] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 2 Further, an accident is not translated except by the translation of its subject. But the subject of sin is the rational soul. Since, then, the rational soul is not translated by origin, as we find in Lib. of Eccl. dogmas, it seems that no sin is contracted by origin.

[61914] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 3 But it must be said that although the subject of sin is not translated, the flesh is nevertheless translated, which is the cause of sin. because when they are placed, no effect is placed. But the flesh is not a sufficient cause of sin; for no matter how much the flesh entices to sin, it is still in the power of the will to consent or not to consent; and thus the will itself is a sufficient cause of sin. But the will is not translated. Therefore the transfer of the flesh is not sufficient for the transfer of any sin.

[61915] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 4 Further, sin, as it is now accepted, is to whom punishment and rebuke are due. But no rebuke and punishment is due to any defect contracted from the origin: for as the Philosopher says in Ethic. but he is reprimanded if he is blind from drunkenness. Therefore no defect which is contracted from the origin has the character of sin.

[61916] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 5 Further, Augustine distinguishes two kinds of evil in 1 On free will: one that we do, which is the evil of guilt, and another that we suffer, which belongs to the evil of punishment. But every deficiency which is from another has the aspect of suffering; for passion is the effect and inference of action. Therefore nothing contracted by origin from another has the character of sin, but only the character of punishment.

[61917] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 6 Further, in Lib. It is said of ecclesiastical dogmas: Our flesh is good, since it was created by a good God. But good is not the cause of evil, according to Matt. 7, 18: a tree cannot produce good fruit that is bad. Therefore original sin is not contracted through the origin of the flesh.

[61918] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 7 Further, the soul depends more on the flesh after it is united to it than on its union itself. But after the soul is already united to the flesh, it cannot be infected by the flesh except by its consent. Therefore, neither in the union itself. Therefore original sin cannot be contracted through the origin of the flesh.

[61919] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Objection 8. Further, if a vitiated origin of the flesh causes sin in the soul, the more vitiated by its origin, the greater the sin it will cause. But in those who are born of fornication, the origin is more defective than in those who are born of legitimate marriage. It would therefore follow that those who are born from fornication contract a greater sin by being born; which is evidently false: because no greater punishment is due to them.

[61920] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, if original sin is contracted through the origin of the flesh, this is only in so far as the flesh is corrupted. Then that corruption is either moral or natural. But it cannot be moral: because the subject of moral corruption is not the flesh, but the soul. Similarly, neither is the natural: because it follows that it infects the soul with natural activity, that is, through active and passive qualities; which is clearly false. In no way, therefore, is sin contracted through the origin of the flesh.

[61921] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 10 Further, the defect which resulted from the sin of the first parent is the lack of original justice, as Anselm says; and so since the original justice is something spiritual, it follows that the aforesaid deficiency is also spiritual. But the corruption of the flesh is something corporeal. But the spiritual and the corporeal are of different kinds; and thus the spiritual cannot cause a bodily effect. Therefore, the corruption in our flesh could not have been caused by the sin of the first parent, from which sin was transfused into us through the origin.

[61922] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, according to Augustine, original sin is the lack of original justice. Either then the original justice belonged to the soul of the first man naturally from his own creation, or it was an added gift from divine liberality. But if it had been a natural soul, it would never have lost it by sinning: because, as Dionysius says, chapter 4. of Div. Nom., natural data also remained in the demons; and thus also all men would have original justice: because what is natural to one soul is natural to all souls; and thus no one would be born with original sin, that is, with a lack of original righteousness. But if that justice was a gift added from divine liberality: then either God gives that gift to the soul of man being born, or not. If he gives, man is not born with a lack of original justice, nor can his soul be infected by the flesh. But if it is not given by God, this does not seem to be imputed to him, but to God, who did not give. In no way, therefore, can man contract original sin.

[61923] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 12 Further, the rational soul does not come upon any pre-existing form: because it does not come to matter as a substantial form, but as accidental matter, which comes to a subject already existing in act. It is necessary, therefore, that when the rational soul arrives, all pre-existing forms should fail, and consequently all accidents. Therefore the corruption of the seed also ceases, if it was inherent in the progenitor. Therefore the coming soul cannot be defiled by the flesh.

[61924] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 13 Further, motion follows the nature of the predominant element in mixed bodies, and consequently all the properties result from that which predominates in the compound. But the soul predominates over the body in man, which is composed of both; but the soul has purity from its origin. Although, therefore, the flesh has contracted some impurity from its origin, it seems that a person who is born should not be said to be infected with sin, but pure.

[61925] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 14. Further, there is a sin to which some punishment is due: but a sin which is contracted through the origin, no punishment is due; for the lack of divine vision, which is commonly assigned to him as a punishment, does not seem to be any kind of punishment; because if a man died without all sin, and had no grace, he would not be able to reach the divine vision, in which eternal life consists, according to John 17, v. 3: this is eternal life, that they may know you alone as the true God; and the Apostle says, Rom. 6, 23: eternal life by the grace of God. Therefore there is no sin which is contracted by origin.

[61926] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, just as the first cause is more noble than the second, so the second cause is more noble than the effect. But if sin is transmitted from the first parent, corruption has followed in the flesh through the soul of the first man who sinned, and it is brought from the flesh to the soul of the man who is born from Adam; and thus the soul of the first man is like the first cause, and the flesh like the second cause, and the soul of the man begotten like the last effect. Thus, then, the soul of the first man will be more noble, and the flesh more noble than the soul of the first man; which is inappropriate. Therefore, sin cannot be transmitted by origin.

[61927] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 16 Further, he does nothing except in so far as he actually is. But there is no actual sin in the seed. Therefore, the soul cannot be infected with any sin through the seed that has been cut.

[61928] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 17 Further, the cause of the infection of sin and merit cannot be the same. But the act of generation can sometimes be meritorious; for example, when a man existing in grace goes to his wife for the purpose of begetting children, or to repay a debt. Therefore the infection of sin in the offspring cannot be caused from this.

[61929] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 18 Further, a particular cause does not bring about a universal effect. But Adam's sin was a particular one. Therefore he could not infect the whole human nature with any sin.

[61930] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 19 Further, the Lord says Ezek. 18, v. 4: All souls are mine; and verse 30: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. But it would bear, if for the sin of the first man those who are born from him were condemned. Therefore sin is not transferred to Adam's descendants because of her sin.

[61931] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. 1 Sed contra. Est quod dicitur, Rom. V, v. 12: through one man sin entered into this world. Sed non per imitationem; because thus sin entered the world through the Devil, according to Wisdom. II, 24-25: the envy of the Devil, death entered the world. Let those who are from his side imitate him. Therefore, through a vitiated origin, sin is derived from the first man to posterity.

[61932] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. Objection 2. Further, Augustine says in Chapter 14 of the City of God that the first man, being depraved of his own accord, begat depraved children. But perversion does not take place except through sin. Therefore the children of Adam contract sin from their origin.

[61933] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 co. I answer It must be said that the Pelagians denied that any sin could be transmitted through origin. But this to a great extent excludes the necessity of the redemption effected by Christ, which seems to have been most necessary to abolish the infection of sin, which was derived from the first parent into all his posterity, as the apostle says, Rom. 5:18, that just as by the offense of one there is a process on all men to condemnation, so also by the righteousness of one on all men to the justification of life. The necessity of baptizing children is also excluded, which is nevertheless a common custom of the Church derived from the apostles, as Dionysius says in the Ecclesiastical Hierar. And therefore it must be said simply that sin is transmitted by origin from the first parent to the posterity. For the evidence of which we must consider that a singular person can be considered in two ways: in the first way, according to the fact that he is a certain singular person; in another way, according to the fact that it is a part of some college, and in both ways an act may belong to it. For it belongs to him in so far as he is a singular person, that act which he does of his own free will and by himself; but in so far as he is a part of the college, any act which he does not do by himself or of his own free will, but which is done by the whole college, or by several of the college, or by the leader of the college, may belong to him. just as what the ruler of the state does, the state is said to do, as the philosopher says. For such a college of men is regarded as one man, so that different men are appointed to different offices as if they were different members of one natural body, as the Apostle says about the members of the Church, 1 Cor. 12, 12. Thus, therefore, the whole multitude of men who receive human nature from their first parent, is to be considered as one college, or rather as one body of one man; in which multitude each man, even Adam himself, may be considered either as a singular person, or as some member of this multitude, which is derived by natural origin from one. Now it must be considered that the first man, in his institution, had been divinely given a certain supernatural gift, namely, original justice, by which reason was subject to God, and the lower powers of reason, and the body of the soul. Now this gift had not been given to the first man as a singular person only, but as a certain principle of the whole human nature, namely, that it should be derived from him through the origin to posterity. But this gift received by the first man, by sinning through his free will, he lost in the manner in which it had been given to him, that is, for himself and for all his posterity. Therefore, the failure of this gift affects all his posterity; and thus this defect is transmitted to posterity in the same way as human nature is transmitted; which indeed is translated not according to itself as a whole, but according to some part of itself, that is, according to the flesh, into which God infuses the soul; and thus, just as the divinely infused soul belongs to the human nature derived from Adam, because of the flesh to which it is united; so also the aforesaid defect pertains to the soul because of the flesh, which is propagated from Adam not only according to the corpulent substance, but also according to the seminal reason, that is, not only materially, but as from an active principle: for thus the son receives from the father the human nature. If, therefore, this defect is considered to have been derived in this way by origin in that man, according to the fact that this man is a kind of singular person, then this kind of defect cannot have the character of guilt, for the character of which it is required that it be voluntary. But if this man begotten be considered as a certain member of the whole human nature propagated by the first parent, as if all men were one man, then he has the reason of guilt because of his voluntary principle, which is the actual sin of the first parent. as if we were to say that the movement of the hand to commit murder, according as the hand is considered by itself, has no reason for guilt, because the hand is necessarily moved by another. But if it be considered that he is a part of the whole man, who acts by his will, he has the reason of guilt, because he is thus voluntary. Just as, then, murder is not called the fault of the hand, but the fault of the whole man; Thus a deficiency of this kind is not said to be a personal sin, but a sin of the whole nature. nor does it pertain to the person, except in so far as nature infects the person. And just as different parts of man are used to commit one sin, namely the will, the reason, the hands, and the like, and yet there is only one sin because of the unity of the principle, namely the will, from which the reason for sin is derived for all the acts of the parts. so also by reason of the principle in all human nature it is considered as one original sin; propter quod apostolus dicit, Rom. V, 12: in quo omnes peccaverunt; which, according to Augustine, can be understood in which namely the first man, or in which sin of the first man, so that the sin of the first man is as it were the common sin of all.

[61934] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 1 To the first reply, therefore, that a sin which is contracted by origin is said to be voluntary by reason of its principle, namely, the will of the first parent, as has been said.

[61935] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 2 To the second reply, that this sin follows the whole human nature; whence the subject of this sin is the soul, inasmuch as it is a part of human nature: and therefore as human nature is transgressed, although the soul is not transgressed; so even original sin is transferred, although the soul is not transferred.

[61936] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 3 Reply to Objection 3: The flesh is not a sufficient cause of actual sin, but it is a sufficient cause of original sin. just as the transmigration of the flesh is a sufficient cause, however materially, of human nature.

[61937] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 4 Reply to the fourth, that what is contracted by origin is not due punishment and rebuke if it is referred to a person, because in this way it does not have the aspect of the will, but if it is related to nature, it has the aspect of the will, as has been said, and in this way rebuke and punishment are due to it.

[61938] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 5. To the fifth answer, that a deficiency by the origin of a contract indeed has the aspect of existing from another, if it is referred to a person, but not if it is referred to a nature. for it is so, as it were, from an intrinsic principle.

[61939] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 6. To the sixth answer, that our flesh is good in its own nature, but inasmuch as it is deprived of original justice because of the sin of the first parent, so it causes original sin.

[61940] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 7. To the seventh answer, that, as has been said, original sin, speaking in itself, is a sin of the nature, not of the person, but by reason of the infected nature. Now the act of generation properly serves nature, because it is directed to the preservation of the species; but the fact that the flesh is already united to the soul belongs to the constitution of the person; and therefore the flesh causes original sin more as it is considered in the way of generation than as it is already united.

[61941] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 8. To the eighth answer, that in those who are born of fornication, it is indeed twofold in origin, viz., the vice of nature, which is transmitted from Adam, and the vice of the person, that is, the begetting father, from which vice no infection is left in the offspring. For everyone who begets transmits original sin to the extent that he generates like Adam, not to the extent that he generates like Peter or Martin; that is by what he has from Adam, not by what is proper to him.

[61942] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 9. To the ninth answer, that the corruption which is in the flesh is indeed a natural act, but by intention and moral virtue. For from the sin of the first parent his flesh was deprived of that virtue, so that from it the seed may be dropped by which the original righteousness is propagated to others; and thus in the seed the lack of this virtue is the lack of moral corruption, and a kind of intention thereof; as we say that the concentration of color is in the air, and the concentration of the soul is in the seed. And from this also there is virtue for a similar imperfection, just as there is virtue for the production of human nature in offspring.

[61943] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 10. To answer the tenth, that nothing prevents a spiritual cause from causing a corporeal effect. For Boethius also says in his book on the Trinity that the forms which are in matter came from the forms which are without matter: and in us the lower appetite is moved by the will, to the movement of which bodily transformation follows.

[61944] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 11 Regarding the eleventh answer, that the original justice was added to the first man out of divine liberality; but what is not given to this soul by God is not on his part, but on the part of human nature, in which the contrary is found preventing.

[61945] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 12. Regarding the twelfth answer, that the corruption of original sin is in the seed, not actually but by virtue, in the same way that human nature is there by virtue: which virtue is active in the seed in the foaming spirit, as Aristotle says in Lib. of Gen. of animals, but not in matter which loses one form and receives another.

[61946] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 13 Regarding the thirteenth point, as Dionysius says in chapter 4. of Div. Nom., good occurs from a whole whole cause, but evil also results from individual defects; and therefore the deficiency which is in the part of the body is sufficient to take away the integrity of human nature.

[61947] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 14. To the fourteenth answer, that the lack of divine vision befits a person in two ways. On the one hand, this is because he does not have in himself the means by which he can reach the divine vision, and thus the lack of divine vision would belong to him who was in the natural sun even without sin. for thus the lack of the divine vision is not a punishment, but a deficiency consequent upon all created nature: for no creature of its natural nature can attain to the divine vision. In another way, the lack of divine vision may belong to someone in this way, that he has something in himself from which it is due to him that he lacks divine vision; and thus the lack of divine vision is the punishment of both original and actual sin.

[61948] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 15 The fifteenth point is that the cause is twofold. One of the principal things that acts through its own form, and this is more noble than the effect in so far as it is the cause. There is another instrumental cause which does not act through its own form, but in so far as it is moved by another, and this need not be more noble in its effect, just as a saw is not more noble than a house. But in this way the carnal seed is the cause of the human nature in the offspring, and also of the original guilt in his soul.

[61949] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 16 To answer the sixteenth, that any agent is in act in many ways. In the first way, according to the proper form, which either contains the form of the effect according to the likeness of the species, just as fire begets fire; or according to power only, as the sun generates fire. In another way, according to motion from another; and in this way the instrument acts as an actual being: and so also the seed is actually, in so far as there is in it the movement and intention of the generative soul, according to the philosopher in Lib. of Gen. of animals; and from this he has the power of causing both human nature and original sin.

[61950] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 17 To the seventeenth answer, that a man, by approaching his wife justly, deserves according to what is proper to him; and so he does not transmit original sin, but according to what he has from Adam, as was said above.

[61951] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 18. To answer the eighteenth, that Adam, in so far as he was the principle of human nature, had the idea of a universal cause, and thus by his act the whole of human nature, which is propagated by him, was corrupted.

[61952] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 19 To answer the nineteenth, that the sin of the first man is in a way the common sin of the whole human nature, as has been said; and therefore when a man is punished for the sin of his first parent, he is not punished for the sin of another, but for his own sin.
en.text: [61911] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 tit. 2 And it seems not. [61912] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 1 For it is called Ecclesi. 15, 18: before man life and death, good and evil: whatsoever he will, it shall be given him. From this it may be understood that sin, which is the spiritual death of the soul, consists in the will. But nothing that man contracts from his origin consists in his will. Therefore man contracts no sin from his origin. [61913] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 2 Further, an accident is not translated except by the translation of its subject. But the subject of sin is the rational soul. Since, then, the rational soul is not translated by origin, as we find in Lib. of Eccl. dogmas, it seems that no sin is contracted by origin. [61914] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 3 But it must be said that although the subject of sin is not translated, the flesh is nevertheless translated, which is the cause of sin. because when they are placed, no effect is placed. But the flesh is not a sufficient cause of sin; for no matter how much the flesh entices to sin, it is still in the power of the will to consent or not to consent; and thus the will itself is a sufficient cause of sin. But the will is not translated. Therefore the transfer of the flesh is not sufficient for the transfer of any sin. [61915] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 4 Further, sin, as it is now accepted, is to whom punishment and rebuke are due. But no rebuke and punishment is due to any defect contracted from the origin: for as the Philosopher says in Ethic. but he is reprimanded if he is blind from drunkenness. Therefore no defect which is contracted from the origin has the character of sin. [61916] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 5 Further, Augustine distinguishes two kinds of evil in 1 On free will: one that we do, which is the evil of guilt, and another that we suffer, which belongs to the evil of punishment. But every deficiency which is from another has the aspect of suffering; for passion is the effect and inference of action. Therefore nothing contracted by origin from another has the character of sin, but only the character of punishment. [61917] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 6 Further, in Lib. It is said of ecclesiastical dogmas: Our flesh is good, since it was created by a good God. But good is not the cause of evil, according to Matt. 7, 18: a tree cannot produce good fruit that is bad. Therefore original sin is not contracted through the origin of the flesh. [61918] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 7 Further, the soul depends more on the flesh after it is united to it than on its union itself. But after the soul is already united to the flesh, it cannot be infected by the flesh except by its consent. Therefore, neither in the union itself. Therefore original sin cannot be contracted through the origin of the flesh. [61919] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Objection 8. Further, if a vitiated origin of the flesh causes sin in the soul, the more vitiated by its origin, the greater the sin it will cause. But in those who are born of fornication, the origin is more defective than in those who are born of legitimate marriage. It would therefore follow that those who are born from fornication contract a greater sin by being born; which is evidently false: because no greater punishment is due to them. [61920] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, if original sin is contracted through the origin of the flesh, this is only in so far as the flesh is corrupted. Then that corruption is either moral or natural. But it cannot be moral: because the subject of moral corruption is not the flesh, but the soul. Similarly, neither is the natural: because it follows that it infects the soul with natural activity, that is, through active and passive qualities; which is clearly false. In no way, therefore, is sin contracted through the origin of the flesh. [61921] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 10 Further, the defect which resulted from the sin of the first parent is the lack of original justice, as Anselm says; and so since the original justice is something spiritual, it follows that the aforesaid deficiency is also spiritual. But the corruption of the flesh is something corporeal. But the spiritual and the corporeal are of different kinds; and thus the spiritual cannot cause a bodily effect. Therefore, the corruption in our flesh could not have been caused by the sin of the first parent, from which sin was transfused into us through the origin. [61922] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, according to Augustine, original sin is the lack of original justice. Either then the original justice belonged to the soul of the first man naturally from his own creation, or it was an added gift from divine liberality. But if it had been a natural soul, it would never have lost it by sinning: because, as Dionysius says, chapter 4. of Div. Nom., natural data also remained in the demons; and thus also all men would have original justice: because what is natural to one soul is natural to all souls; and thus no one would be born with original sin, that is, with a lack of original righteousness. But if that justice was a gift added from divine liberality: then either God gives that gift to the soul of man being born, or not. If he gives, man is not born with a lack of original justice, nor can his soul be infected by the flesh. But if it is not given by God, this does not seem to be imputed to him, but to God, who did not give. In no way, therefore, can man contract original sin. [61923] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 12 Further, the rational soul does not come upon any pre-existing form: because it does not come to matter as a substantial form, but as accidental matter, which comes to a subject already existing in act. It is necessary, therefore, that when the rational soul arrives, all pre-existing forms should fail, and consequently all accidents. Therefore the corruption of the seed also ceases, if it was inherent in the progenitor. Therefore the coming soul cannot be defiled by the flesh. [61924] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 13 Further, motion follows the nature of the predominant element in mixed bodies, and consequently all the properties result from that which predominates in the compound. But the soul predominates over the body in man, which is composed of both; but the soul has purity from its origin. Although, therefore, the flesh has contracted some impurity from its origin, it seems that a person who is born should not be said to be infected with sin, but pure. [61925] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 14. Further, there is a sin to which some punishment is due: but a sin which is contracted through the origin, no punishment is due; for the lack of divine vision, which is commonly assigned to him as a punishment, does not seem to be any kind of punishment; because if a man died without all sin, and had no grace, he would not be able to reach the divine vision, in which eternal life consists, according to John 17, v. 3: this is eternal life, that they may know you alone as the true God; and the Apostle says, Rom. 6, 23: eternal life by the grace of God. Therefore there is no sin which is contracted by origin. [61926] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, just as the first cause is more noble than the second, so the second cause is more noble than the effect. But if sin is transmitted from the first parent, corruption has followed in the flesh through the soul of the first man who sinned, and it is brought from the flesh to the soul of the man who is born from Adam; and thus the soul of the first man is like the first cause, and the flesh like the second cause, and the soul of the man begotten like the last effect. Thus, then, the soul of the first man will be more noble, and the flesh more noble than the soul of the first man; which is inappropriate. Therefore, sin cannot be transmitted by origin. [61927] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 16 Further, he does nothing except in so far as he actually is. But there is no actual sin in the seed. Therefore, the soul cannot be infected with any sin through the seed that has been cut. [61928] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 17 Further, the cause of the infection of sin and merit cannot be the same. But the act of generation can sometimes be meritorious; for example, when a man existing in grace goes to his wife for the purpose of begetting children, or to repay a debt. Therefore the infection of sin in the offspring cannot be caused from this. [61929] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 18 Further, a particular cause does not bring about a universal effect. But Adam's sin was a particular one. Therefore he could not infect the whole human nature with any sin. [61930] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 19 Further, the Lord says Ezek. 18, v. 4: All souls are mine; and verse 30: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. But it would bear, if for the sin of the first man those who are born from him were condemned. Therefore sin is not transferred to Adam's descendants because of her sin. [61931] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. 1 Sed contra. Est quod dicitur, Rom. V, v. 12: through one man sin entered into this world. Sed non per imitationem; because thus sin entered the world through the Devil, according to Wisdom. II, 24-25: the envy of the Devil, death entered the world. Let those who are from his side imitate him. Therefore, through a vitiated origin, sin is derived from the first man to posterity. [61932] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. Objection 2. Further, Augustine says in Chapter 14 of the City of God that the first man, being depraved of his own accord, begat depraved children. But perversion does not take place except through sin. Therefore the children of Adam contract sin from their origin. [61933] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 co. I answer It must be said that the Pelagians denied that any sin could be transmitted through origin. But this to a great extent excludes the necessity of the redemption effected by Christ, which seems to have been most necessary to abolish the infection of sin, which was derived from the first parent into all his posterity, as the apostle says, Rom. 5:18, that just as by the offense of one there is a process on all men to condemnation, so also by the righteousness of one on all men to the justification of life. The necessity of baptizing children is also excluded, which is nevertheless a common custom of the Church derived from the apostles, as Dionysius says in the Ecclesiastical Hierar. And therefore it must be said simply that sin is transmitted by origin from the first parent to the posterity. For the evidence of which we must consider that a singular person can be considered in two ways: in the first way, according to the fact that he is a certain singular person; in another way, according to the fact that it is a part of some college, and in both ways an act may belong to it. For it belongs to him in so far as he is a singular person, that act which he does of his own free will and by himself; but in so far as he is a part of the college, any act which he does not do by himself or of his own free will, but which is done by the whole college, or by several of the college, or by the leader of the college, may belong to him. just as what the ruler of the state does, the state is said to do, as the philosopher says. For such a college of men is regarded as one man, so that different men are appointed to different offices as if they were different members of one natural body, as the Apostle says about the members of the Church, 1 Cor. 12, 12. Thus, therefore, the whole multitude of men who receive human nature from their first parent, is to be considered as one college, or rather as one body of one man; in which multitude each man, even Adam himself, may be considered either as a singular person, or as some member of this multitude, which is derived by natural origin from one. Now it must be considered that the first man, in his institution, had been divinely given a certain supernatural gift, namely, original justice, by which reason was subject to God, and the lower powers of reason, and the body of the soul. Now this gift had not been given to the first man as a singular person only, but as a certain principle of the whole human nature, namely, that it should be derived from him through the origin to posterity. But this gift received by the first man, by sinning through his free will, he lost in the manner in which it had been given to him, that is, for himself and for all his posterity. Therefore, the failure of this gift affects all his posterity; and thus this defect is transmitted to posterity in the same way as human nature is transmitted; which indeed is translated not according to itself as a whole, but according to some part of itself, that is, according to the flesh, into which God infuses the soul; and thus, just as the divinely infused soul belongs to the human nature derived from Adam, because of the flesh to which it is united; so also the aforesaid defect pertains to the soul because of the flesh, which is propagated from Adam not only according to the corpulent substance, but also according to the seminal reason, that is, not only materially, but as from an active principle: for thus the son receives from the father the human nature. If, therefore, this defect is considered to have been derived in this way by origin in that man, according to the fact that this man is a kind of singular person, then this kind of defect cannot have the character of guilt, for the character of which it is required that it be voluntary. But if this man begotten be considered as a certain member of the whole human nature propagated by the first parent, as if all men were one man, then he has the reason of guilt because of his voluntary principle, which is the actual sin of the first parent. as if we were to say that the movement of the hand to commit murder, according as the hand is considered by itself, has no reason for guilt, because the hand is necessarily moved by another. But if it be considered that he is a part of the whole man, who acts by his will, he has the reason of guilt, because he is thus voluntary. Just as, then, murder is not called the fault of the hand, but the fault of the whole man; Thus a deficiency of this kind is not said to be a personal sin, but a sin of the whole nature. nor does it pertain to the person, except in so far as nature infects the person. And just as different parts of man are used to commit one sin, namely the will, the reason, the hands, and the like, and yet there is only one sin because of the unity of the principle, namely the will, from which the reason for sin is derived for all the acts of the parts. so also by reason of the principle in all human nature it is considered as one original sin; propter quod apostolus dicit, Rom. V, 12: in quo omnes peccaverunt; which, according to Augustine, can be understood in which namely the first man, or in which sin of the first man, so that the sin of the first man is as it were the common sin of all. [61934] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 1 To the first reply, therefore, that a sin which is contracted by origin is said to be voluntary by reason of its principle, namely, the will of the first parent, as has been said. [61935] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 2 To the second reply, that this sin follows the whole human nature; whence the subject of this sin is the soul, inasmuch as it is a part of human nature: and therefore as human nature is transgressed, although the soul is not transgressed; so even original sin is transferred, although the soul is not transferred. [61936] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 3 Reply to Objection 3: The flesh is not a sufficient cause of actual sin, but it is a sufficient cause of original sin. just as the transmigration of the flesh is a sufficient cause, however materially, of human nature. [61937] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 4 Reply to the fourth, that what is contracted by origin is not due punishment and rebuke if it is referred to a person, because in this way it does not have the aspect of the will, but if it is related to nature, it has the aspect of the will, as has been said, and in this way rebuke and punishment are due to it. [61938] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 5. To the fifth answer, that a deficiency by the origin of a contract indeed has the aspect of existing from another, if it is referred to a person, but not if it is referred to a nature. for it is so, as it were, from an intrinsic principle. [61939] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 6. To the sixth answer, that our flesh is good in its own nature, but inasmuch as it is deprived of original justice because of the sin of the first parent, so it causes original sin. [61940] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 7. To the seventh answer, that, as has been said, original sin, speaking in itself, is a sin of the nature, not of the person, but by reason of the infected nature. Now the act of generation properly serves nature, because it is directed to the preservation of the species; but the fact that the flesh is already united to the soul belongs to the constitution of the person; and therefore the flesh causes original sin more as it is considered in the way of generation than as it is already united. [61941] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 8. To the eighth answer, that in those who are born of fornication, it is indeed twofold in origin, viz., the vice of nature, which is transmitted from Adam, and the vice of the person, that is, the begetting father, from which vice no infection is left in the offspring. For everyone who begets transmits original sin to the extent that he generates like Adam, not to the extent that he generates like Peter or Martin; that is by what he has from Adam, not by what is proper to him. [61942] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 9. To the ninth answer, that the corruption which is in the flesh is indeed a natural act, but by intention and moral virtue. For from the sin of the first parent his flesh was deprived of that virtue, so that from it the seed may be dropped by which the original righteousness is propagated to others; and thus in the seed the lack of this virtue is the lack of moral corruption, and a kind of intention thereof; as we say that the concentration of color is in the air, and the concentration of the soul is in the seed. And from this also there is virtue for a similar imperfection, just as there is virtue for the production of human nature in offspring. [61943] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 10. For Boethius also says in his book on the Trinity that the forms which are in matter came from the forms which are without matter: and in us the lower appetite is moved by the will, to the movement of which bodily transformation follows. document:aquinas-sth:iii-45-4-ad-2.contentHtml:
Latin

Ad secundum dicendum quod sicut in Baptismo, ubi declaratum fuit mysterium primae regenerationis, ostensa est operatio totius Trinitatis, per hoc quod fuit ibi filius incarnatus, apparuit spiritus sanctus in specie columbae, et pater fuit ibi declaratus in voce; ita etiam in transfiguratione, quae est sacramentum secundae regenerationis, tota Trinitas apparuit, pater in voce, filius in homine, spiritus sanctus in nube clara; quia sicut in Baptismo dat innocentiam, quae per simplicitatem columbae designatur, ita in resurrectione dabit electis suis claritatem gloriae et refrigerium ab omni malo, quae designantur in nube lucida.

English

Reply to Objection 2: Just as in the Baptism, where the mystery of the first regeneration was proclaimed, the operation of the whole Trinity was made manifest, because the Son Incarnate was there, the Holy Ghost appeared under the form of a dove, and the Father made Himself known in the voice; so also in the transfiguration, which is the mystery of the second regeneration, the whole Trinity appears---the Father in the voice, the Son in the man, the Holy Ghost in the bright cloud; for just as in baptism He confers innocence, signified by the simplicity of the dove, so in the resurrection will He give His elect the clarity of glory and refreshment from all sorts of evil, which are signified by the bright cloud.

document:aquinas-creed:10.translationNote: Open-source bilingual Latin and English text.
document:aquinas-creed:10.contentHtml:
Latin

ARTICLE 10

sanctorum communionem, remissionem peccatorum

Bonum ergo Christi communicatur omnibus Christianis, sicut virtus capitis omnibus membris;

et haec communicatio fit per sacramenta Ecclesiae, in quibus operatur virtus passionis Christi, quae operatur ad conferendam gratiam in remissionem peccatorum. Huiusmodi autem sacramenta Ecclesiae sunt septem.

Primum est Baptismus, qui est regeneratio quaedam spiritualis. Sicut enim vita carnalis non potest haberi nisi homo carnaliter nascatur: ita vita spiritualis, vel gratiae, non potest haberi nisi homo renascatur spiritualiter. Haec autem generatio fit per Baptismum: Ioan. III, 5: nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei. Et est sciendum, quod sicut homo non nascitur nisi semel, sic et semel tantum baptizatur: unde et sancti addiderunt: confiteor unum Baptisma. Virtus autem Baptismi est quod purgat ab omnibus peccatis et quantum ad culpam et quantum ad poenam: et inde est quod nulla poenitentia imponitur baptizatis, quantumcumque fuerint peccatores; et si statim moriantur post Baptismum, immediate evolant in vitam aeternam. Inde est etiam quod licet soli sacerdotes ex officio baptizent, ex necessitate tamen cuilibet licet baptizare, servata tamen forma Baptismi, quae est: ego te baptizo in nomine patris et filii et spiritus sancti. Sumit autem hoc sacramentum virtutem a passione Christi: Rom. VI, 5: quicumque baptizati sumus in Christo Iesu, in morte ipsius baptizati sumus. Et inde est quod sicut Christus fuit tribus diebus in sepulcro, ita fit trina immersio in aqua.

Secundum sacramentum est confirmatio. Sicut enim in illis qui corporaliter nascuntur, necessariae sunt vires ad operandum; ita spiritualiter renatis necessarium est robur spiritus sancti. Unde et apostoli ad hoc quod essent fortes, receperunt spiritum sanctum post ascensionem Christi: Luc. XXIV, 49: vos autem sedete in civitate, quousque induamini virtute ex alto. Hoc autem robur confertur in sacramento confirmationis: et ideo illi qui habent curam puerorum, debent multum esse soliciti quod confirmentur, quia in confirmatione confertur magna gratia. Et si decedet, maiorem habet gloriam confirmatus quam non confirmatus, quia hic habuit plus de gratia.

Tertium sacramentum est Eucharistia. Sicut enim in vita corporali, postquam homo natus est et vires sumpsit, necessarius est ei cibus, ut conservetur et sustentetur; ita in vita spirituali post habitum robur necessarius est ei cibus spiritualis, qui est corpus Christi. Ioan. VI, 54: nisi manducaveritis carnem filii hominis et biberitis eius sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Et ideo secundum ordinationem Ecclesiae quilibet Christianus semel in anno debet recipere corpus Christi, digne tamen et munde: quia, ut dicitur I Cor. XI, 29, qui manducat et bibit indigne, scilicet cum conscientia peccati mortalis de quo non est confessus, vel non proponit abstinere, iudicium sibi manducat et bibit.

Quartum sacramentum est poenitentia. Contingit enim in vita corporali quod quandoque quis infirmatur, et nisi habeat medicinam, moritur; et ita in vita spirituali quis infirmatur per peccatum: unde necessaria est medicina ad recuperandam sanitatem. Et haec est gratia quae confertur in poenitentiae sacramento. Psal. CII, 3: qui propitiatur omnibus iniquitatibus tuis, qui sanat omnes infirmitates tuas. In poenitentia autem tria debent esse: contritio, quae est dolor de peccato cum proposito abstinendi; confessio peccatorum cum integritate: et satisfactio quae est per bona opera.

Quintum sacramentum est extrema unctio. In hac enim vita sunt multa quae impediunt, propter quae homo non potest perfecte consequi purgationem a peccatis. Et quia nullus potest intrare vitam aeternam nisi sit bene purgatus, necessarium fuit aliud sacramentum quo homo purgaretur a peccatis, et liberaretur ab infirmitate, et praepararetur ad introitum regni caelestis. Et hoc est sacramentum extremae unctionis. Sed quod non semper curet corporaliter, hoc est quia forte vivere non expedit saluti animae. Iac. V, 14-15: infirmatur quis in vobis? Inducat presbyteros Ecclesiae, et orent super eum, ungentes eum oleo in nomine domini: et oratio fidei salvabit infirmum, et alleviabit eum dominus; et si in peccatis sit, remittentur ei. Sic ergo patet quod per quinque sacramenta quae praedicta sunt, habetur perfectio vitae.

Sed quia necessarium est quod huiusmodi sacramenta conferantur per determinatos ministros, ideo fuit necessarium sacramentum ordinis, cuius ministerio huiusmodi sacramenta dispensarentur. Nec est attendenda ad hoc eorum vita, si aliquando ad mala declinant; sed virtus Christi, per quam ipsa sacramenta efficaciam habent, quorum ipsi dispensatores sunt: apostolus, I Cor. IV, 1: sic nos existimet homo ut ministros Christi, et dispensatores mysteriorum Dei; et hoc est sextum sacramentum, scilicet ordinis.

Septimum sacramentum est matrimonium, in quo si munde vivunt, homines salvantur, et possunt sine peccato mortali vivere. Et interdum declinant coniugati ad venialia, quando eorum concupiscentia non fertur extra bona matrimonii; et si efferatur extra, tunc declinant ad mortale.

Per haec autem septem sacramenta consequimur peccatorum remissionem. Et ideo hic statim subditur: remissionem peccatorum. Per hoc etiam datum est apostolis dimittere peccata. Et ideo credendum est quod ministri Ecclesiae, ad quos derivata est huiusmodi potestas ab apostolis, et ad apostolos a Christo, in Ecclesia habeant potestatem ligandi atque solvendi, et quod in Ecclesia sit plena potestas dimittendi peccata, sed gradatim, scilicet a Papa in alios praelatos.

Sciendum est etiam, quod non solum virtus passionis Christi communicatur nobis, sed etiam meritum vitae Christi. Et quidquid boni fecerunt omnes sancti, communicatur in caritate existentibus, quia omnes unum sunt: Psal. CXVIII, 63: particeps ego sum omnium timentium te. Et inde est quod qui in caritate vivit, particeps est omnis boni quod fit in toto mundo; sed tamen specialius illi pro quibus specialius fit aliquod bonum. Nam unus potest satisfacere pro alio, sicut patet in beneficiis, ad quae plures congregationes admittunt aliquos. Sic ergo per hanc communionem consequimur duo: unum scilicet quod meritum Christi communicatur omnibus; aliud quod bonum unius communicatur alteri. Unde excommunicati, per hoc quod sunt extra Ecclesiam, perdunt partem omnium bonorum quae fiunt; quod est maius damnum quam damnum alicuius rei temporalis. Est etiam aliud periculum: quia constat quod per huiusmodi suffragia impeditur Diabolus ne possit nos tentare: unde quando quis excluditur ab huiusmodi suffragiis, Diabolus facilius vincit eum. Et inde est quod in primitiva Ecclesia, cum aliquis excommunicabatur, statim Diabolus vexabat eum corporaliter.

ARTICLE 10

“The Communion of Saints, the Forgiveness of Sins.”

As in our natural body the operation of one member works for the good of the entire body, so also is it with a spiritual body, such as is the Church. Because all the faithful are one body, the good of one member is communicated to another: “And every one members, one of another” [Rm 12:5]. So, among the points of faith which the Apostles have handed down is that there is a common sharing of good in the Church. This is expressed in the words, “the Communion of Saints”. Among the various members of the Church, the principal member is Christ, because He is the Head: “He made Him head over all the Church, which is His body” [Eph 1:22]. Christ communicates His good, just as the power of the head is communicated to all the members.

This communication takes place through the Sacraments of the Church in which operate the merits of the passion of Christ, which in turn operates for the conferring of grace unto the remission of sins. These Sacraments of the Church are seven in number.

“Baptism.”—The first is Baptism which is a certain spiritual regeneration. Just as there can be no physical life unless man is first born in the flesh, so spiritual life or grace cannot be had unless man is spiritually reborn. This rebirth is effected through Baptism: “Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” [Jn 3:5]. It must be known that, just as a man can be born but once, so only once is he baptized. Hence, the holy Fathers put into the Nicene Creed: “I confess one baptism.” The power of Baptism consists in this, that it cleanses from all sins as regards both their guilt and their punishment. For this reason no penance is imposed on those who are baptized, no matter to what extent they had been sinners. Moreover, if they should die immediately after Baptism, they would without delay go to heaven. Another result is that, although only priests “ex officio” may baptize, yet any one may baptize in case of necessity, provided that the proper form of Baptism is used. This is: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” This Sacrament receives its power from the passion of Christ. “All we who are baptized in Christ Jesus are baptized in His death” [Rm 6:3]. Accordingly there is a threefold immersion in water after the three days in which Christ was in the sepulchre.

“Confirmation.”—The second Sacrament is Confirmation. Just as they who are physically born need certain powers to act, so those who are reborn spiritually must have the strength of the Holy Spirit which is imparted to them in this Sacrament. In order that they might become strong, the Apostles received the Holy Spirit after the Ascension of Christ: “Stay you in the city till you be endowed with power from on high” [Lk 24:49]. This power is given in the Sacrament of Confirmation. They, therefore, who have the care of children should be very careful to see that they be confirmed, because great grace is conferred in Confirmation. He who is confirmed will, when he dies, enjoy greater glory than one not confirmed, because greater grace will be his.

“Holy Eucharist.”—The Eucharist is the third Sacrament. In the physical life, after man is born and acquires powers, he needs food to sustain and strengthen him. Likewise in the spiritual life, after being fortified, he has need of spiritual food; this is the Body of Christ: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink His blood, you shall not have life in you “[Jn 6:54]. According to the prescribed law of the Church, therefore, every Christian must at least once a year receive the Body of Christ, and in a worthy manner and with a clean conscience: “For he who eats and drinks unworthily [that is, by being conscious of unconfessed mortal sin on his soul, or with no intent to abstain from it] eats and drinks judgment to himself” [1 Cor 11:29].

“Penance.”—The fourth Sacrament is Penance. In the physical life, one who is sick and does not have recourse to medicine, dies; so in the spiritual order, one becomes ill because of sin. Thus, medicine is necessary for recovery of health; and this is the grace which is conferred in the Sacrament of Penance: “Who forgives all your iniquities; who heals all your diseases” [Ps 102:3]. Three things must be present in the Sacrament of Penance: contrition, which is sorrow for sin together with a resolution not to sin again; confession of sins, as far as possible entire; and satisfaction which is accomplished by good works.

“Extreme Unction.”—Extreme Unction is the fifth Sacrament. In this life there are many things which prevent one from a perfect purification from one’s sins. But since no one can enter into eternal life until he is well cleansed, there is need of another Sacrament which will purify man of his sins, and both free him from sickness and prepare him for entry into the heavenly kingdom. This is the Sacrament of Extreme Unction. That this Sacrament does not always restore health to the body is due to this, that perhaps to live is not to the advantage of the soul’s salvation. “Is any man sick amongst you? Let him bring in the priests of the Church and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith shall save the sick man. And the Lord shall raise him up; and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him” [James 5:14-15]. It is now clear that the fullness of life is had from these five Sacraments.

“Holy Orders.”—It is necessary that these Sacraments be administered by chosen ministers. Therefore, the Sacrament of Orders is necessary, by whose powers these Sacraments are dispensed. Nor need one note the life of such ministers, if here and there one fail in his office, but remember the virtue of Christ through whose merits the Sacraments have their efficacy, and in whose Name the ministers are but dispensers: “Let a man so account of us as of the ministers of Christ and the dispensers of the mysteries of God” [1 Cor 4:1]. This then is the sixth Sacrament, namely, Orders.

“Matrimony.”—The seventh Sacrament is Matrimony, and in it men, if they live uprightly, are saved; and thereby they are enabled to live without mortal sin. Sometimes the partners in marriage fall into venial sin, when their concupiscence does not extend beyond the rights of matrimony; but if they do go beyond such rights, they sin mortally.

By these seven Sacraments we receive the remission of sins, and so in the Creed there follows immediately: “the forgiveness of sins.” The power was given to the Apostles to forgive sins. We must believe that the ministers of the Church receive this power from the Apostles; and the Apostles received it from Christ; and thus the priests have the power of binding and loosing. Moreover, we believe that there is the full power of forgiving sins in the Church, although it operates from the highest to the lowest, i.e., from the Pope down through the prelates.

We must also know that not only the efficacy of the Passion of Christ is communicated to us, but also the merits of His life; and, moreover, all the good that all the Saints have done is communicated to all who are in the state of grace, because all are one: “I am a partaker of all those who fear You” [Ps 118:63]. Therefore, he who lives in charity participates in all the good that is done in the entire world; but more specially does he benefit for whom some good work is done; since one man certainly can satisfy for another. Thus, through this communion we receive two benefits. One is that the merits of Christ are communicated to all; the other is that the good of one is communicated to another. Those who are excommunicated, however, because they are cut off from the Church, forfeit their part of all the good that is done, and this is a far greater loss than being bereft of all material things. There is a danger lest the devil impede this spiritual help in order to tempt one; and when one is thus cut off, the devil can easily overcome him. Thus it was in the primitive Church that, when one was excommunicated, the devil even physically attacked him.

ARTICLE 10

sanctorum communionem, remissionem peccatorum

Bonum ergo Christi communicatur omnibus Christianis, sicut virtus capitis omnibus membris;

et haec communicatio fit per sacramenta Ecclesiae, in quibus operatur virtus passionis Christi, quae operatur ad conferendam gratiam in remissionem peccatorum. Huiusmodi autem sacramenta Ecclesiae sunt septem.

Primum est Baptismus, qui est regeneratio quaedam spiritualis. Sicut enim vita carnalis non potest haberi nisi homo carnaliter nascatur: ita vita spiritualis, vel gratiae, non potest haberi nisi homo renascatur spiritualiter. Haec autem generatio fit per Baptismum: Ioan. III, 5: nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei. Et est sciendum, quod sicut homo non nascitur nisi semel, sic et semel tantum baptizatur: unde et sancti addiderunt: confiteor unum Baptisma. Virtus autem Baptismi est quod purgat ab omnibus peccatis et quantum ad culpam et quantum ad poenam: et inde est quod nulla poenitentia imponitur baptizatis, quantumcumque fuerint peccatores; et si statim moriantur post Baptismum, immediate evolant in vitam aeternam. Inde est etiam quod licet soli sacerdotes ex officio baptizent, ex necessitate tamen cuilibet licet baptizare, servata tamen forma Baptismi, quae est: ego te baptizo in nomine patris et filii et spiritus sancti. Sumit autem hoc sacramentum virtutem a passione Christi: Rom. VI, 5: quicumque baptizati sumus in Christo Iesu, in morte ipsius baptizati sumus. Et inde est quod sicut Christus fuit tribus diebus in sepulcro, ita fit trina immersio in aqua.

Secundum sacramentum est confirmatio. Sicut enim in illis qui corporaliter nascuntur, necessariae sunt vires ad operandum; ita spiritualiter renatis necessarium est robur spiritus sancti. Unde et apostoli ad hoc quod essent fortes, receperunt spiritum sanctum post ascensionem Christi: Luc. XXIV, 49: vos autem sedete in civitate, quousque induamini virtute ex alto. Hoc autem robur confertur in sacramento confirmationis: et ideo illi qui habent curam puerorum, debent multum esse soliciti quod confirmentur, quia in confirmatione confertur magna gratia. Et si decedet, maiorem habet gloriam confirmatus quam non confirmatus, quia hic habuit plus de gratia.

Tertium sacramentum est Eucharistia. Sicut enim in vita corporali, postquam homo natus est et vires sumpsit, necessarius est ei cibus, ut conservetur et sustentetur; ita in vita spirituali post habitum robur necessarius est ei cibus spiritualis, qui est corpus Christi. Ioan. VI, 54: nisi manducaveritis carnem filii hominis et biberitis eius sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Et ideo secundum ordinationem Ecclesiae quilibet Christianus semel in anno debet recipere corpus Christi, digne tamen et munde: quia, ut dicitur I Cor. XI, 29, qui manducat et bibit indigne, scilicet cum conscientia peccati mortalis de quo non est confessus, vel non proponit abstinere, iudicium sibi manducat et bibit.

Quartum sacramentum est poenitentia. Contingit enim in vita corporali quod quandoque quis infirmatur, et nisi habeat medicinam, moritur; et ita in vita spirituali quis infirmatur per peccatum: unde necessaria est medicina ad recuperandam sanitatem. Et haec est gratia quae confertur in poenitentiae sacramento. Psal. CII, 3: qui propitiatur omnibus iniquitatibus tuis, qui sanat omnes infirmitates tuas. In poenitentia autem tria debent esse: contritio, quae est dolor de peccato cum proposito abstinendi; confessio peccatorum cum integritate: et satisfactio quae est per bona opera.

Quintum sacramentum est extrema unctio. In hac enim vita sunt multa quae impediunt, propter quae homo non potest perfecte consequi purgationem a peccatis. Et quia nullus potest intrare vitam aeternam nisi sit bene purgatus, necessarium fuit aliud sacramentum quo homo purgaretur a peccatis, et liberaretur ab infirmitate, et praepararetur ad introitum regni caelestis. Et hoc est sacramentum extremae unctionis. Sed quod non semper curet corporaliter, hoc est quia forte vivere non expedit saluti animae. Iac. V, 14-15: infirmatur quis in vobis? Inducat presbyteros Ecclesiae, et orent super eum, ungentes eum oleo in nomine domini: et oratio fidei salvabit infirmum, et alleviabit eum dominus; et si in peccatis sit, remittentur ei. Sic ergo patet quod per quinque sacramenta quae praedicta sunt, habetur perfectio vitae.

Sed quia necessarium est quod huiusmodi sacramenta conferantur per determinatos ministros, ideo fuit necessarium sacramentum ordinis, cuius ministerio huiusmodi sacramenta dispensarentur. Nec est attendenda ad hoc eorum vita, si aliquando ad mala declinant; sed virtus Christi, per quam ipsa sacramenta efficaciam habent, quorum ipsi dispensatores sunt: apostolus, I Cor. IV, 1: sic nos existimet homo ut ministros Christi, et dispensatores mysteriorum Dei; et hoc est sextum sacramentum, scilicet ordinis.

Septimum sacramentum est matrimonium, in quo si munde vivunt, homines salvantur, et possunt sine peccato mortali vivere. Et interdum declinant coniugati ad venialia, quando eorum concupiscentia non fertur extra bona matrimonii; et si efferatur extra, tunc declinant ad mortale.

Per haec autem septem sacramenta consequimur peccatorum remissionem. Et ideo hic statim subditur: remissionem peccatorum. Per hoc etiam datum est apostolis dimittere peccata. Et ideo credendum est quod ministri Ecclesiae, ad quos derivata est huiusmodi potestas ab apostolis, et ad apostolos a Christo, in Ecclesia habeant potestatem ligandi atque solvendi, et quod in Ecclesia sit plena potestas dimittendi peccata, sed gradatim, scilicet a Papa in alios praelatos.

Sciendum est etiam, quod non solum virtus passionis Christi communicatur nobis, sed etiam meritum vitae Christi. Et quidquid boni fecerunt omnes sancti, communicatur in caritate existentibus, quia omnes unum sunt: Psal. CXVIII, 63: particeps ego sum omnium timentium te. Et inde est quod qui in caritate vivit, particeps est omnis boni quod fit in toto mundo; sed tamen specialius illi pro quibus specialius fit aliquod bonum. Nam unus potest satisfacere pro alio, sicut patet in beneficiis, ad quae plures congregationes admittunt aliquos. Sic ergo per hanc communionem consequimur duo: unum scilicet quod meritum Christi communicatur omnibus; aliud quod bonum unius communicatur alteri. Unde excommunicati, per hoc quod sunt extra Ecclesiam, perdunt partem omnium bonorum quae fiunt; quod est maius damnum quam damnum alicuius rei temporalis. Est etiam aliud periculum: quia constat quod per huiusmodi suffragia impeditur Diabolus ne possit nos tentare: unde quando quis excluditur ab huiusmodi suffragiis, Diabolus facilius vincit eum. Et inde est quod in primitiva Ecclesia, cum aliquis excommunicabatur, statim Diabolus vexabat eum corporaliter.
